deep.reconstruction:
Context: this page continues the tables of the previous and next pages, which belong to Gauss's theory of biquadratic (quartic) residues. For each prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) Gauss gives:
- a primitive root g;
- f with f^2 ≡ -1 (mod p);
- the decomposition p = a^2 + b^2, normalised so that a ≡ 1 (mod 4) and a + b f ≡ 0 (mod p). This is the same convention as on the neighbouring pages, e.g. 277: 9 + 14·217 ≡ 0.
- the four classes A, B, C, D of residues. A class is fixed by ind_g(x) mod 4, which is 0, 1, 2, 3 respectively. A is the set of biquadratic residues and C the quadratic residues that are not quartic.

(1) p = 233 = 13^2 + 8^2, g = 3, f = 144.
- 144^2 = 20736 = 89·233 - 1, so f^2 ≡ -1.
- 8·144 = 1152 ≡ -13, so a + b f ≡ 0.
- 233 ≡ 1 (mod 8), so -1 lies in A. Each class is therefore closed under x → -x, and Gauss lists only 1..116.
- Each class has 29 entries, and 4 × 29 = 116.
- Consistency: 3 ∈ B, 9 ∈ C, 27 ∈ D, 81 ∈ A. Also 2 ∈ A, in agreement with Gauss's criterion that 2 is a quartic residue iff p = x^2 + 64y^2; here 233 = 13^2 + 64·1^2.

(2) p = 229 = 15^2 + 2^2, g = 6, f = 122, a = -15, b = +2.
- 122^2 = 14884 = 65·229 - 1.
- 2·122 = 244 ≡ 15 = -a.
- 229 ≡ 5 (mod 8), so -1 has index 114 ≡ 2 and lies in C. Hence x ∈ A ⇔ -x ∈ C, and x ∈ B ⇔ -x ∈ D. Listing 1..114 is again sufficient.
- Counts: A 29, B 35, C 28, D 22. So A + C = 57 and B + D = 57, as required.
- Checks: 6 ∈ B, 36 ∈ C, 6^4 ≡ 151 = -78 with 78 ∈ C, so 6^4 ∈ A. The vertical bars in rows B and D are working marks; the items 18 and 47 were inserted later.

(3) Bottom half: empirical tables for the quartic character of a fixed prime q, taken with the sign that makes it primary: -23, -19, +17, +13. The moduli are all primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) from 5 to 293 (29 primes, with q itself omitted).
- Left column: the p sorted by the class (A–D) of q mod p.
- Right column: for each p, the residue r ≡ b/a (mod q), with ∞ when q | a and 0 when q | b.
- My verification (all agree), for q = 23:
  - 13 = (-3)^2 + 2^2 gives 2/(-3) ≡ 7.
  - 41 gives 13; 101 gives 10; 233 gives 8/13 ≡ 13; 257 (a = 1, b = -16) gives 7.
  - D row: 17 → 19, 61 → 8, 109 → 12, 181 → 19, 229 → 2/(-15) ≡ 6.
- The small numbers set apart on the right (16.0.∞; 4; 1.14; 20.21; 0.17; ∞; 1; 0; 0) are the residues r not realised in the data. Gauss adds them to complete each class, as if he were partitioning the whole projective line of ratios mod q.
- The completed partitions:
  - q = -23 (24 points, 6 per class): A = {0, ∞, ±7, ±10}, B = {2, 3, 4, 11, 15, 17}, C = {±1, ±5, ±9}, D = -B.
  - q = -19 (20 points, 5 per class): A = {0, ±2, ±5}, B = {3, 7, 11, 13, 18}, C = {∞, ±4, ±9}, D = -B = {1, 6, 8, 12, 16}.
  - q = 17 (18 points; ±4 = √-1 excluded, 4 per class): A = {0, ∞, ±1}, B = {2, 6, 8, 14}, C = {±5, ±7}, D = -B.
  - q = 13 (14 points; ±5 excluded, 3 per class): A = {0, ±4}, B = {6, 11, 12}, C = {∞, ±3}, D = -B.
- The structure is always the same: A and C are symmetric under r → -r, and D = -B, because conjugating a + bi exchanges B and D.
- This is the empirical form of the theorem that the biquadratic character of q mod p depends only on a + bi mod q, i.e. on b/a. That is the content of the biquadratic reciprocity law (Gauss's 'theorema fundamentale').

Corrected reading of the -23 table: the small inserted primes 241.281.293 belong to row B, not C.
- Their ratios 11, 17, 15 are B-values, and (p/23) = -1 for all three.
- Then A = 5, B = 12, C = 7, D = 5 primes (total 29).
- The right-hand rows have 5, 11, 7, 5 values; the B row omits p = 5, whose ratio is 2.
errors: No arithmetic errors found in the spot checks. Checked: p = a^2 + b^2 and f^2 ≡ -1 for both primes; class membership of g, g^2, g^3, g^4, 2, -1; class counts; about 30 ratio values in the q-tables.
In the -23 table the right-hand B row (11 values) omits p = 5 (ratio 2 mod 23). Consequently the completion note beside B reads only '4', although B also needs 2 (= -21, since 21 is in D).
In the -19 table the last D entry is struck out (illegible). The row is complete without it (6 primes, 6 ratios, total 29).
'107.1' in row D of p = 229 is a stray mark; the next entries 109 and 112 belong to D.

results.what: Tables of the four biquadratic residue classes A, B, C, D (indices mod 4) for p = 233 and 229, with primitive root, √-1 mod p and normalised p = a^2 + b^2 (a ≡ 1 mod 4, a + bf ≡ 0)
results.modern_name: Quartic residue character / index classes mod 4; primary decomposition of p in Z[i]

results.what: Empirical determination of the quartic character of q = -23, -19, 17, 13 mod p as a function of b/a mod q, with completion of the partition of the projective line mod q
results.modern_name: Biquadratic reciprocity law: [q/p]_4 depends only on a+bi mod q (criteria in terms of p = a^2+b^2)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (statement 1832; induction in Nachlass); proofs Jacobi (lectures 1836-37), Eisenstein 1844; explicit criteria for small q also Dirichlet, Lebesgue

deep.surprise_reason: These are computational tables of exactly the kind known from Gauss's Nachlass (Werke II/X) on biquadratic residues. They show the inductive route to biquadratic reciprocity, which Gauss is already credited with discovering. The completed partition of ratios mod q is a nice detail but not new.
